turns.summary: Splarf wakes at The Thinning to a settlement gripped by the Water Crisis and whispers of something stirring beneath the world's crafts.
turns.narration:
You wake to the sound of the veil thinning. Not a sound that ears hear — a sound that runs through the bones, a tone that slides between the notes, a presence-made-audible. The Thinning is waking up.

The lean-to you've sheltered in for the night sits at the edge of the settlement, where buildings give way to grass and the grass gives way to the thin places where the world gets negotiable. Morning light here doesn't fall straight. It bends. The air tastes like copper and honeysuckle, flavors that don't belong to spring. Through the open doorway you can see Boo — or the shadow-shape that is probably Boo — sitting exactly where it was when you slept, watching the space between the trees where something used to be.

Folk are moving in the settlement behind you, voices taut and practical. You catch fragments as you roll from your bedroll: boiled water, upstream, sick families. The Water Crisis has reached this far. But there's something else underneath it — a tremor in how people are speaking, a word that keeps surfacing: substrate. Something under everything is coming back online.

Boo's head turns toward the deeper wood. Toward the veil.

turns.player: Follow Boo's gaze into the space between the trees — see what the dark has already found.
turns.summary: You wake to the veil singing and find something that came through it — a figure half-real, reading the valley, standing in the thin place where the waygate breathes.
turns.narration:
You push yourself up on your elbows and follow Boo's unblinking stare into the space between the trees.

At first there is nothing — just the bent light, the copper taste, the settlement's sounds distant behind you. Then your eyes adjust, and the space resolves into something that was ALWAYS there and your waking mind had simply refused to hold it.

A figure stands in the thin place where the trees open onto the waygate clearing. They are not quite solid. Light passes through them the way light passes through water — bent, but moving. Their shape is human enough to recognize and wrong enough to make your breath catch: too many joints in the arms, a posture that suggests they are standing and falling simultaneously, a face that shifts when you look at it directly — not changing, but revealing, layer by layer, that there was always more to see.

Boo's ears — both of them, though you were certain a moment ago there was only one — rotate toward you. A statement: *This one came through.*

The figure does not move. Does not seem to see you. But the air around them hums with the same tone that woke you this morning, and you understand with sudden clarity that they are *reading* the valley the way you read a page — taking in everything at once, learning the shape of it. The veil is not just thin here. It is open. And something on the other side has noticed that it can step through.

bio.hometown: Crestfall Notch, a wind-scoured saddle pass in the upper Harmonic Heights where the ridge-currents create near-constant low resonance — not a proper Heights settlement, just a handful of families who serviced the old relay infrastructure before the De-technologizing and then simply stayed, growing root vegetables in terraced shelves cut into the rock face
bio.residence: A rented lean-to workshop bolted to the outer wall of a granary on the valley floor, in the loose market settlement of Dirtmouth Crossing — drafty, cluttered with half-repaired tools, but his; he sleeps on a cot wedged between a workbench and a wall hung with other people's broken things
bio.livelihood: Itinerant mending — he walks a rotating circuit of valley-floor farms and lower-Heights outposts, fixing what the De-technologizing left behind: hand pumps, ox harnesses, millstone housings, the occasional photonic lamp whose crystal mount has cracked. He charges in grain, meal, or coin, whatever a household can spare
bio.hobbies: Rough-stone carving (he carries a small chisel and works river cobbles into dense, unpretty animal shapes while he walks); load-bearing — he voluntarily takes on the heaviest physical labor he can find in each settlement, less for pay than for the clean satisfaction of it; and a quiet habit of sitting near the Heights resonance vents at dusk to listen, though he could not explain why
bio.motivation: The family that took Splarf in after his parents died — a mending woman named Hoss and her elderly father — lost their Notch lease two winters ago to a resource claim filed by a Heights tone-guild asserting ancestral acoustic rights over the pass. Splarf watched Hoss pack everything she owned into a single cart and walk downhill without a word. He wants to find the specific document, the specific clerk, the specific decision that made that legal — not to overturn the world, just to understand exactly how a family gets erased on paper, and whether anything can be written back
bio.story: Splarf was left at Crestfall Notch as an infant — no note, no name anyone recognized — and raised communally by the pass families until Hoss formally took him in at age four. He grew into the kind of person a settlement leans on without noticing: the one who re-digs the drainage channel before anyone else sees it flooding, who carries the injured neighbor down three switchbacks without complaint. When the tone-guild eviction came, his physical capability meant nothing against ink and seal, and that specific helplessness lodged in him like a splinter. He has spent two years on the valley circuit now, fixing things and quietly asking questions of anyone who has dealt with guild claims, Plateau light-law, or valley-floor common-right traditions — building, slowly and without a plan, toward the moment he understands enough to do something that actually counts.

chronicleCache.text: You have become the kind of person who keeps a question like a stone in the pocket — worn smooth from handling, never set down. When the tone-guild's claim took the Notch lease two winters ago, you stood in the doorway and watched Hoss load everything she and her father owned into a single cart, and she never looked back, and you have not stopped looking since. The specific document. The specific clerk. The specific signature that made a family erasable. You are barely known to the Numinous, a stranger to everyone else, carrying nothing of consequence yet — only that question, and the particular grief of someone who lost his first parents and then, very quietly, lost his second ones too.
